title: Microbiology of Artisanal Cheese
excerpt: The biochemical ecology of affineur aging caves: lactic acid bacteria cascades, Penicillium roqueforti lipolysis, Brevibacterium linens smear rinds, and amino acid crystals.
author: Chef Mateo Silva
imageAlt: Wheels of aged artisanal raw milk cheese resting on untreated wooden aging cave shelves

body.text: The Living Architecture of Ripening Caves

Transforming perishable fluid milk into an aged, complex cheese like Parmigiano Reggiano or Roquefort is an exercise in microbiological choreography. Inside natural aging caves with stable humidity and temperature, affineurs cultivate successions of bacteria, yeasts, and filamentous molds that dismantle milk fats and proteins into intensely savory aroma compounds.
Key Ripening Microorganisms and Chemical Transformations

items: Starter Lactic Acid Bacteria (LAB): Lactococcus and Streptococcus converting lactose into lactic acid, dropping pH to expel whey curds.
Secondary Proteolysis: Endogenous and bacterial enzymes breaking hydrophobic casein proteins into savory glutamate and crunchy tyrosine crystals.
Penicillium roqueforti & Lipolysis: Blue molds breaking triglycerides into methyl ketones (such as 2-heptanone), creating sharp, peppery flavors.
Brevibacterium linens: The red-orange bacteria of washed-rind cheeses synthesizing methanethiol and volatile sulfur compounds responsible for pungent aromas.

body.text: A great cheese wheel is not an inert food product; it is a complex living ecosystem where microclimates shape hundreds of distinct chemical volatile bouquets.

body.text: Cheeses crafted from unpasteurized raw milk retain the indigenous pasture microflora of grazing cattle, sheep, or goats, creating non-replicable terroir notes that industrially pasteurized cultures cannot match.
